slides.title: Duplicate a cue, then edit only the duplicate
keyPoints: A group contains several cue kinds
The copy starts with the same visible value
Later edits must leave the original alone
slides.narration: Imagine a presentation tool with a text cue and a list cue. The user duplicates the group, then changes the first name in the copied list. They expect the original list to remain unchanged. This requirement includes more than obtaining another pointer. We need another object with the same starting value and the same kind of behavior, plus independent editable data. If the caller already knows the exact type, normal C++ value copying may be all we need. The difficult case is a mixed collection whose caller sees only the shared Cue interface. Prototype will let each actual object decide how to duplicate itself through that interface.
actions: Ask learners what Duplicate should mean in a presentation editor.
Separate same starting value from same object identity.

question.prompt: What three properties must a successful cue duplicate have?
question.answer: It starts with the same public value, preserves the concrete cue behavior, and supports independent edits according to the copy contract.

slides.title: Same value and same identity are different claims
keyPoints: Equal text does not prove independent storage
A new owner does not automatically mean a deep copy
Define which mutable data must be independent
slides.narration: Two cue objects can both display Start without being the same object. Conversely, two handles can have different variable names while both reach one object. Identity asks whether we are dealing with one entity or two. Value asks what that entity currently contains or does. Our duplicate command needs distinct identities with equal initial public values. It also needs independence for the editable names. These are separate properties, so they need separate checks. If a future cue shares an immutable image, sharing that image may be acceptable even while names remain independent. We must say where the copy boundary lies before declaring that a clone is deep enough.
actions: Give examples of two equal values and two aliases to one value.
Ask what resources a cue could safely share.

question.prompt: Do equal text results alone prove that two cues can be edited independently?
question.answer: No. Two handles can point to the same cue and report equal text. An edit-and-observe test is needed to demonstrate independence.

slides.title: Known value types already know how to copy
keyPoints: A vector of strings copies its values
Editing the copied list does not edit the original
Clearing the original does not empty the copy
slides.narration: This example needs no inheritance or clone operation. CueList holds a vector of strings, and the compiler-provided copy copies that vector. The strings are value objects, so later edits are independently observable. The first output remains Check, the second is Inspect, and clearing the original list still leaves Inspect in the copy. front returns the first element; our initialization and copy guarantee the copied list is nonempty when front is used. The lesson is to begin with ordinary copying when the concrete type is known. Prototype becomes useful only when a caller must ask an unknown concrete type behind a common interface to make the right copy.
actions: Predict all three output lines before Run.
Identify the invariant that makes front safe for the copied list.

question.prompt: Why is copy.names.front still valid after original.names.clear?
question.answer: The copied vector owns its own string values and is still nonempty. Clearing the original does not clear the copy.

slides.title: Copying a shared handle does not duplicate the list
keyPoints: The first edit changes the original
The second copy allocates a distinct list
Sharing is legal but violates independent-edit requirements
slides.narration: Here the first copy is a copy of a shared_ptr handle. Both handles keep one list alive. Editing through handle_copy therefore changes what original sees, and the first line reports Inspect. Nothing is dangling and there is no undefined behavior. The mistake is a mismatch with the user's requirement for independent edits. The second construction copies the list value into a new object. Changing that new list to Continue leaves the old one at Inspect. Replacing a noncopyable unique_ptr with shared_ptr merely to make compilation succeed can create exactly this defect. Select an ownership policy because it matches the required meaning of duplication, not because it silences an error.

question.prompt: Is the shared-handle version broken memory management?
question.answer: No. It manages shared lifetime correctly, but it violates the independent-edit contract by keeping one mutable list behind both handles.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Duplicate cues through the Cue interface without selecting concrete constructors in the loop.
Preserve concrete behavior and initial public values.
Keep originals unchanged after valid and rejected edits of clones.
slides.narration:
Duplicate mixed presentation cues with independent edits. Each concrete cue implements clone with its own copy constructor. Value-owned strings and vectors give independent editable state, while unique_ptr states ownership of each new polymorphic object.

Duplicate cues through the Cue interface without selecting concrete constructors in the loop. Preserve concrete behavior and initial public values. Keep originals unchanged after valid and rejected edits of clones.

clone returns a new owner of the same concrete kind and equivalent initial value. A successful rename preserves nonempty names. Cloned editable contents do not alias originals. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. Ordinary copying is simpler for a container of one known value type. A variant of a closed set of cue types can also support value copying without a virtual clone. Prototype fits an extensible hierarchy whose concrete types are unknown to the duplication code.

question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: clone returns a new owner of the same concrete kind and equivalent initial value. A successful rename preserves nonempty names. Cloned editable contents do not alias originals.

slides.title: The limitation is lost concrete type information
keyPoints: A unique_ptr cannot be copied because copying the sole owner would give two owners responsibility for deleting one object.
The Prototype pattern asks the existing object to create that copy.
slides.narration:
A unique_ptr cannot be copied because copying the sole owner would give two owners responsibility for deleting one object. Copying Cue itself would not solve the problem either. Cue is abstract here, so it cannot be constructed. In a nonabstract hierarchy, copying only the base part can discard derived data and behavior, a problem called object slicing. Neither copying the handle nor copying only the base subobject means “make an independent object of the same actual kind.”

The Prototype pattern asks the existing object to create that copy. Cue declares a virtual clone operation returning a new owning Cue handle. TextCue and ListCue each know their own concrete type, so each can call its own copy constructor. The caller asks for a clone without deciding which constructor to invoke. Prototype is therefore about construction from an existing object’s state, not simply about any function named copy.

slides.title: What clone preserves
keyPoints: ListCue::clone calls make_unique<ListCue>(*this).
The clone’s type is still ListCue even though its returned owner is unique_ptr<Cue>.
During compilation, the compiler generates the appropriate memberwise copy constructor and checks the clone override signature.
slides.narration:
ListCue::clone calls make_unique<ListCue>(*this). this points at the current ListCue; *this refers to the whole current ListCue object. Inside a const member, that expression is a const reference suitable for copying. The explicitly defaulted copy constructor copies the vector member. Both concrete cue types declare their copy constructors this way, suppressing implicit object moves. Constructing from an rvalue therefore copies instead of emptying the source; moves of unique_ptr handles still transfer ownership without moving the cue object itself. Copying a vector of strings copies each string value, so the clone owns independent character data in the normal observable sense. Editing one list’s first name does not edit the other list’s name.

The clone’s type is still ListCue even though its returned owner is unique_ptr<Cue>. Later virtual calls to text and rename reach ListCue behavior. The new object has a different address but starts with the same public value. Equal value and shared identity are different ideas: two clocks can display the same time without being the same clock. The program checks both equal initial text and distinct object addresses.

During compilation, the compiler generates the appropriate memberwise copy constructor and checks the clone override signature. During execution, the actual cue chooses which clone override runs. Allocation creates new storage, construction copies the concrete object into it, and ownership returns to the caller. If copying fails, make_unique cleans up the allocated storage; the original remains owned by its existing handle.

slides.title: Copy depth is a design decision
keyPoints: A shallow copy copies a handle or address while keeping the same underlying resource.
A unique_ptr member normally makes the containing type noncopyable until a copy operation is explicitly defined.
Some resources should not be cloned at all.
slides.narration:
A shallow copy copies a handle or address while keeping the same underlying resource. A deep copy makes an independent copy of owned contents, to the depth promised by the application. The words need a boundary. A vector of strings gives independent string values. A vector of shared_ptr<Image> would copy handles and share images unless the clone explicitly copied them. That may be correct if images are immutable and expensive, but it would not be correct for an independently editable image promise.

A unique_ptr member normally makes the containing type noncopyable until a copy operation is explicitly defined. The lab adds BoxCue with a unique_ptr<string>. Its copy constructor allocates a new string initialized from the original string. Simply returning make_unique<BoxCue>(*this) without that copy constructor would fail to compile. Replacing unique_ptr with shared_ptr just to silence the error would change ownership meaning and make edits visible through both handles.

Some resources should not be cloned at all. A live socket, open transaction, mutex, or hardware session has an identity that copying bytes cannot duplicate. A clone may copy configuration while opening a fresh session, share a documented immutable resource, or reject duplication. Cyclic object graphs need additional rules: a map from old objects to new objects can preserve internal relationships without infinite recursion. Do not promise a universal deep copy without defining where the copy stops.

slides.title: Keep the generic loop simple and the copy rules local
keyPoints: The loop over originals uses const auto& because each vector element is a unique_ptr and must not be copied.
Each new owner goes into copies.
Prototype is useful for user duplication, reusable configured objects, and heterogeneous snapshots when copying has a clear domain meaning.
slides.narration:
The loop over originals uses const auto& because each vector element is a unique_ptr and must not be copied. The reference borrows the owning handle; const prevents reseating that handle through this reference. It does not by itself make the pointed-to object const. clone is separately declared const to promise that cloning does not mutate the cue’s ordinary members. The arrow calls the operation on the object reached through the handle.

Each new owner goes into copies. push_back accepts the returned temporary owning handle by move. After the loop, originals and copies are separate owning collections. Destruction of either collection destroys only its own objects. The program renames the first entry of the copied ListCue and checks that the original text is still list:Check;Begin; while the copied text becomes list:Inspect;Begin;.

Prototype is useful for user duplication, reusable configured objects, and heterogeneous snapshots when copying has a clear domain meaning. A registry may keep named prototypes and return clones, but the registry is optional. If the concrete type is already known and ordinary value copying works, use it. If objects should have unique noncopyable identities, omit clone instead of adding a misleading operation. Maintaining a clone requires adding new fields to its copy policy as the type evolves, especially when members change from values to owning or shared handles.

question.prompt: When is Prototype unnecessary?
question.answer: When callers know the concrete type and ordinary value copying already expresses the requirement. Prototype helps copy through a common interface without naming every concrete kind.

slides.title: Ask the object that knows its own concrete type
keyPoints: Cue declares a virtual clone operation
ListCue invokes its own copy constructor
The client receives a new unique_ptr<Cue>
slides.narration: The generic client knows only Cue, so it cannot safely choose between TextCue and ListCue constructors. Each concrete cue already knows its own type. A virtual clone operation moves that decision to the object that has the information. When the client calls clone through a Cue handle, execution selects the actual cue's override. ListCue then creates a new ListCue copied from itself and returns ownership through the Cue interface. That is Prototype: construction from the state of an existing object without the client naming its concrete type. The caller can keep one simple duplication loop as new cue kinds arrive, while each cue maintains its own copy policy.

question.answer: The concrete object knows its actual type. Keeping that knowledge local avoids a type switch that every new cue would need to extend.

theory.what: Virtual copying preserves the actual object kind behind a common interface.
theory.where: Cue::clone is implemented by TextCue, ListCue, and the extension BoxCue.
theory.why: A mixed-cue caller cannot name every concrete copy constructor.
theory.invariant: A clone begins with equivalent public value and the promised independence.
theory.risk: Copying a base value or a shared mutable handle can lose behavior or independence.

slides.title: An owning handle is not the object value
keyPoints: unique_ptr cannot be copied into a second sole owner
Moving a handle transfers ownership
Copying a base subobject can lose derived information
slides.narration: A unique_ptr is a handle with sole cleanup responsibility. Copying it would create two supposed sole owners, so the language forbids that operation. Moving it is allowed, but a move transfers the same object to another owner; it does not duplicate the object. Another tempting idea is to copy the Cue value itself. This chapter's Cue is abstract, so that cannot be constructed at all. In a nonabstract hierarchy, copying just the base part can discard derived fields and behavior, a problem called slicing. clone solves a different operation from both handle transfer and base copying: it constructs another complete object of the same actual kind with its own owner.
actions: Compare the verbs borrow, transfer, and duplicate.
Ask which one a user’s Duplicate command requires.

question.prompt: Does std::move on a unique_ptr create a duplicate cue?
question.answer: No. It transfers ownership of the same cue and leaves the source handle empty. A duplicate needs a separately constructed object.

slides.title: Read make_unique<ListCue>(*this) one part at a time
keyPoints: this points to the current concrete object
*this refers to that complete object
The concrete copy constructor defines the new contents
slides.narration: Inside ListCue::clone, this points to the current ListCue. The leading star in *this gives a reference to that object. Because clone is const, it supplies a const source for copying. make_unique<ListCue> allocates storage and constructs a ListCue using that source, which selects the copy constructor. The chapter explicitly defaults the copy constructor, so the vector member is copied using its normal value behavior. The returned handle converts to unique_ptr<Cue>, but the allocated object remains a ListCue. Later text and rename calls therefore still use list behavior. If allocation or construction fails, the construction helper does not leave an ownerless successfully allocated object behind.
actions: Read the construction expression aloud from inside outward.
Distinguish the type of the handle from the type of the object it owns.

question.prompt: Does returning unique_ptr<Cue> change the newly allocated object from ListCue into Cue?
question.answer: No. The owner exposes the base interface, while the complete object and its virtual behavior remain ListCue.

slides.title: The loop borrows each owner and stores each new owner
keyPoints: The colon means iterate over originals
const auto& avoids copying a unique_ptr
The returned owner moves into copies
slides.narration: In for (const auto& cue : originals), the colon means take each element from originals in turn. auto infers the element's type. The ampersand borrows the element rather than copying its unique_ptr, and const stops us from reseating that owner through this reference. An important subtlety remains: a const unique_ptr does not by itself make the pointed-to object const. The clone operation is separately const to express that it should not change the cue's ordinary state. Each clone returns a temporary owning handle, and push_back transfers that handle into copies. At the end, each collection owns its own objects and can be destroyed independently.
actions: Explain every piece of the range-based loop declaration.
Ask which const applies to the owner and which applies to clone.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch04.json → Keep the generic loop simple and the copy rules local

question.prompt: What would go wrong with for (auto cue : originals) for this vector?
question.answer: It attempts to copy each unique_ptr element, which is forbidden. Borrowing each owner with a reference avoids that build error.

slides.title: A new resource member requires a new copy decision
keyPoints: A unique_ptr member blocks implicit copying
BoxCue explicitly duplicates its owned string
Some resources should remain noncopyable
slides.narration: The extension adds BoxCue, whose name lives in a uniquely owned string. Memberwise copying cannot copy that unique_ptr. BoxCue therefore supplies a copy constructor that allocates a new string containing the old string's value. After that, clone can use make_unique<BoxCue>(*this) normally. This is a local repair based on the member's ownership meaning. A socket, mutex, or open transaction needs more thought: copying bytes does not create a second valid session or lock. A clone might copy configuration and establish a fresh resource, share a documented immutable asset, or be unavailable. Whenever a new field arrives, review what copying that field should mean and how a test will show it.
actions: Describe the BoxCue copy constructor’s two separate allocations in source and clone.
Ask for one resource that cannot sensibly be copied as raw bytes.

question.prompt: Why is replacing BoxCue’s unique_ptr<string> with shared_ptr<string> not an equivalent repair?
question.answer: It changes independent ownership into shared mutable state. Editing the clone could then change the original, violating the promised copy behavior.

Copy assignment is not required by this lab’s interface and is not supplied; a real type should document or implement its desired assignment policy rather than assume clone implies every copy operation exists.

Keep clone policy beside the concrete type. Review every newly added pointer-like member for whether it should copy deeply, share immutable state, or forbid cloning.

question.prompt: Explain Prototype without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Each concrete cue implements clone with its own copy constructor. Value-owned strings and vectors give independent editable state, while unique_ptr states ownership of each new polymorphic object. Ordinary copying is simpler for a container of one known value type. A variant of a closed set of cue types can also support value copying without a virtual clone. Prototype fits an extensible hierarchy whose concrete types are unknown to the duplication code.

slides.title: Test independence through edits and destruction
keyPoints: Check equal starting text
Edit the clone and inspect both objects
Destroy the original and use the clone again
slides.narration: A clone test should exercise the promise in stages. First compare public values immediately after cloning. Then edit the clone and confirm the original is unchanged. Check a rejected edit too, because an invalid empty name must not damage the clone's existing value. Finally destroy the original and use the clone again. That last step exposes a clone that merely borrowed storage from the old object. The BoxCue extension demonstrates this with Open and Close: the copied cue remains box:Close after the original owner is reset. No single check replaces the others. Distinct addresses alone do not prove that nested mutable resources were also copied independently.
actions: Ask students to order the four tests from initial value to lifetime independence.
Name the hidden defect each test can expose.

question.prompt: Why is a different object address insufficient evidence of a deep-enough copy?
question.answer: Two outer objects can still share the same nested mutable data. Edit and lifetime tests must cover the resources that the contract says are independent.

slides.title: Use Prototype when duplication has a real meaning
keyPoints: Known concrete values can use ordinary copying
Heterogeneous duplication benefits from clone
Unique identities may forbid copying entirely
slides.narration: Prototype fits a mixed collection of editable values when Duplicate is a meaningful user operation. It may also fit a library of preconfigured objects that clients copy and customize. A registry of named prototypes is optional; the core mechanism is still virtual copying from an existing object. If the concrete type is already known and its value members copy correctly, direct copying is simpler. If an object represents a unique live transaction, pretending it can be cloned may be misleading. You can also choose a closed value representation such as a variant when the type set is known and that makes copying clearer. Begin with the domain's duplication meaning, then choose the mechanism that preserves it.

question.prompt: Does every class hierarchy need clone?
question.answer: No. Add it only when independent duplication is a meaningful supported operation. Some identities should remain noncopyable.

comparisons.label: Ordinary copy
comparisons.text: Use for a known concrete value whose members already have the right copy behavior.

comparisons.label: Virtual clone
comparisons.text: Use when a caller must duplicate unknown concrete kinds through a shared interface.

comparisons.label: No copying
comparisons.text: Use when identity or external-resource rules make duplication invalid.

slides.title: Recall what is copied, what is shared, and why
keyPoints: The actual object selects its copy constructor
The caller receives a new owner
Copy depth is part of the public contract
slides.narration: Explain the chapter without using the word deep as a shortcut. A ListCue clone contains a new vector of copied string values, so changing a name in one list leaves the other unchanged. A BoxCue clone contains a new allocated string, so destroying the original does not remove the clone's data. These concrete statements are stronger than saying everything is copied. Now imagine adding a large immutable icon and a mutable caption to a cue. Sharing the icon could be reasonable, while the caption must remain independent. State that boundary and write tests for it. That is how Prototype remains maintainable as a simple value grows into a richer object.

question.prompt: For a cue with an immutable shared icon and an editable caption, must every clone duplicate the icon bytes?
question.answer: Not necessarily. The contract can permit immutable icon sharing while requiring an independent caption. The clone implementation and tests must match that stated boundary.
